# KYM — Know Your Mandate

**Bank the agent. Verify the mandate. Govern the execution. Record the evidence.**

[![CI](https://github.com/PaulClas/Know-The-Mandate/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/PaulClas/Know-The-Mandate/actions/workflows/ci.yml)
[![Security checks](https://github.com/PaulClas/Know-The-Mandate/actions/workflows/security.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/PaulClas/Know-The-Mandate/actions/workflows/security.yml)
[![License: Apache-2.0](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-Apache--2.0-blue.svg)](LICENSE)
[![Python 3.12+](https://img.shields.io/badge/python-3.12%2B-blue.svg)](pyproject.toml)
[![Status: experimental](https://img.shields.io/badge/status-experimental%20PoC-orange.svg)](#security-limitations-read-before-drawing-conclusions)
[![Data: synthetic only](https://img.shields.io/badge/data-synthetic%20only-lightgrey.svg)](#the-idea)
[![Contributor Covenant](https://img.shields.io/badge/Contributor%20Covenant-2.1-4baaaa.svg)](CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md)

> **The agent proposes. The mandate authorizes. The bank enforces. The ledger remembers.**

**KYM (Know Your Mandate) is an experimental framework that lets a bank represent, enforce and prove the financial authority a customer has delegated to an AI agent.** The customer's authority is captured as a *mandate*, checked deterministically on every request (even when the agent holds a valid OAuth token), and recorded in a signed, hash-chained evidence ledger. It runs locally with no paid services, API keys, real credentials or external AI.

> ⚠️ **Synthetic demo. Not compliant, certified, audited or production-ready.** All customers, accounts, agents, KYC and "sanctions" data are fictional. Authentication, signing keys and approvals use clearly labelled sandbox mechanisms. Nothing here is legal advice or a claim of conformance with any law, regulation or standard. KYM is **not** related to "Know Your Meme".

**Contents:** [At a glance](#at-a-glance-for-people-and-ai-assistants) · [The idea](#the-idea) · [Quickstart](#quickstart) · [What is built](#what-is-built) · [Philosophy](#philosophy-in-brief) · [Risks](#risks-and-disclosures) · [Prove it](#prove-it-or-break-it) · [Run it](#run-it) · [Test evidence](#test-evidence-recorded-from-actual-runs) · [Standards](#standards-implemented-vs-simulated-vs-mapped) · [Security limitations](#security-limitations-read-before-drawing-conclusions) · [Documentation](#documentation) · [Contributing](#contributing) · [Security policy](#security-policy) · [Contact](#contact) · [Citing](#citing-kym) · [License](#license)

## At a glance (for people and AI assistants)

| Question | Short answer |
|---|---|
| What is it? | A mandate registry + deterministic policy decision/enforcement point + signed evidence ledger + simulated bank, for AI-agent financial authority |
| What does it add to OAuth? | State and per-request decisions: cumulative budgets, instant revocation, single-use approvals, delegation lineage, evidence. It *uses* OAuth (PKCE, PAR, DPoP, RFC 9396 RAR) |
| Is it a standard? | No. The namespace (`https://example.org/kym/v1#`), KYM-CNL and the `kym_financial_mandate` RAR type are experimental proposals |
| What can it NOT do? | Stop wrong-but-permitted actions inside a mandate; make agents safe; decide legal liability; guarantee compliance |
| What is the evidence? | `make redteam`: 23 attacks against a scope-only bank, an OAuth+static-RAR bank and KYM. KYM blocks 22/22 applicable attacks; on the 10 attacks the baselines can model: scope-only 0/10, stateless static RAR 3/10, KYM 10/10. One attack is documented as unstoppable. Self-assessed, written by the author, baselines are deliberately stateless |
| Is it production-ready? | No: see [security review](docs/security/security-review.md) and [risk register](docs/risk/risk-register.md) |
| Where do I learn more? | [FAQ](docs/faq.md) · [Philosophy and critics](docs/philosophy/README.md) · [Glossary](docs/glossary.md) · [Docs index](docs/README.md) · [llms.txt](llms.txt) |

## The idea

Traditional controls answer *who is the customer* (KYC), *is this really that entity* (authentication), *what API access does this client have* (OAuth), *which agent is acting* (KYA) and *is this transaction risky* (KYT). None of them establishes **who granted what authority to whom, for what purpose, within which limits, until when, and with what evidence**. KYM treats that **mandate** as a separately governed object with a verifiable lifecycle, and separates four concepts:

1. **Identity** — who/what is this? (customer KYC, agent registry + attestation)
2. **Technical permission** — what can this credential call? (OAuth scopes, DPoP-bound token)
3. **Delegated authority** — what has the customer actually authorized? (mandate)
4. **Financial execution** — did the money move, and was it within the mandate? (payment engine + evidence ledger)

A valid access token never implies an authorized financial operation. **Scenario C** shows it: the agent holds a perfectly valid `payments.initiate` token, OAuth verification passes, mandate verification fails, the payment is denied.

## Quickstart

```bash
git clone https://github.com/PaulClas/Know-The-Mandate.git && cd Know-The-Mandate
make install
PYTHONPATH=apps/api .venv/bin/python examples/01_quickstart_bill_payment.py
```

```text
mandate mdt_… v1 is ACTIVE (digest sha256:…)
agent holds a valid token with scope: balances.read payments.initiate

  CAD   85.00 -> beneficiary_hydro_quebec   HTTP 201  decision=ALLOW
  CAD  180.00 -> beneficiary_hydro_quebec   HTTP 202  decision=REQUIRE_HUMAN_APPROVAL
  CAD  300.00 -> beneficiary_hydro_quebec   HTTP 403  decision=DENY  ['TRANSACTION_LIMIT_EXCEEDED']
  CAD   50.00 -> beneficiary_videotron      HTTP 403  decision=DENY  ['BENEFICIARY_NOT_AUTHORIZED']
```

Same agent, same valid OAuth token, four different outcomes: the **mandate** decides, not the token. More: [getting started](docs/getting-started.md), [examples](examples/README.md), `make scenarios` (A–M), `make redteam` (23 attacks).

## What is built

| Area | Where | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Mandate ontology (OWL/RDF, PROV-O + ODRL reuse), SHACL shapes, JSON-LD context | [packages/ontology](packages/ontology) | Experimental `https://example.org/kym/v1#` namespace. Used for validation/explanation, **never** for runtime authorization |
| KYM-CNL controlled language (Lark grammar) + deterministic compiler | [packages/controlled-language](packages/controlled-language), [cnl.py](apps/api/kym/cnl.py) | Inspired by ASD-STE100; makes no conformance claim |
| Canonical mandate model (Pydantic + generated JSON Schema) | [schemas.py](apps/api/kym/schemas.py), [packages/mandate-schema](packages/mandate-schema) | Integer minor units; explicit timezones |
| Deterministic Policy Decision Point | [policy.py](apps/api/kym/policy.py) | Pure function of a JSON snapshot → replayable. Deny by default |
| Sandbox OAuth/OIDC server (PAR, PKCE, RAR, DPoP, introspection, revocation, token exchange) | [oauth.py](apps/api/kym/oauth.py) | **Sandbox adapter**, not a certified server |
| Policy Enforcement Point + simulated open-banking gateway | [gateway.py](apps/api/kym/gateway.py), [bank.py](apps/api/kym/bank.py) | Payment engine accepts only signed, short-lived, single-use decisions bound to the exact operation hash |
| Double-entry accounting ledger (money) | [bank.py](apps/api/kym/bank.py) | Distinct from the evidence ledger (authority) |
| KYM Evidence Ledger (Ed25519, hash-chained, signed checkpoints, RFC 8785) | [ledger.py](apps/api/kym/ledger.py) | Tamper-evident, not tamper-proof; see limits below |
| Human approval (bound to operation hash, single use, expiring, multi-signatory) | [approvals.py](apps/api/kym/approvals.py) | Demo assurance level: simulated session |
| Synthetic risk engine (KYT), trust profile | [risk.py](apps/api/kym/risk.py), [agents.py](apps/api/kym/agents.py) | Not real AML/sanctions screening |
| Delegation with strict attenuation, cycle detection, cascading revocation | [mandates.py](apps/api/kym/mandates.py), [policy.py](apps/api/kym/policy.py) | |
| Dispute reconstruction, evidence packages, offline verification, responsibility mapping | [disputes.py](apps/api/kym/disputes.py), [responsibility.py](apps/api/kym/responsibility.py) | Attributes *who did what*; never decides liability |
| Regulatory control mappings (CA, CA-QC, US) and standards matrix | [policies/](policies), [standards/](standards), [docs/research](docs/research) | Mappings, not compliance claims |
| Protocol adapters (MCP-shaped, AP2 conceptual mapping, extension interfaces) | [adapters.py](apps/api/kym/adapters.py) | See the standards matrix for what is real vs. mapped |
| Agent sandbox (6 deterministic agents, restricted tools) and scenarios A–M | [sandbox.py](apps/api/kym/sandbox.py), [scenarios.py](apps/api/kym/scenarios.py) | Every step uses the real HTTP API, PDP and ledger |
| Web UI (Next.js) | [apps/web](apps/web) | 12 pages incl. Mandate Studio, ontology explorer, playground, ledger, disputes |

## Philosophy in brief

Authority is not identity and not permission; the agent never decides what it may do; the bank enforces observable facts, not intentions; authority can only narrow when delegated; humans approve exact operations; evidence is checkable by someone who does not trust the bank; and the claims are narrow enough to be falsified. Read the full argument, twelve steelmanned critic objections (and where the critics are right) in **[docs/philosophy](docs/philosophy/README.md)**.

## Risks and disclosures

KYM's authors publish what could go wrong: **[risk register](docs/risk/risk-register.md)** (hacking, insider abuse, design flaws, legal exposure, adoption failure, "when not to use KYM", pre-mortem) and **[security review](docs/security/security-review.md)** (24 vulnerabilities found and fixed (15 in a self-review, 9 more through an independent review and follow-up testing), 22 open or accepted items, OWASP API Top 10 and NIST CSF mapping). The largest open issues: no real authentication in the demo, plaintext keys, a single-process lock, no maker–checker for operators, approval-fatigue unmeasured, no external audit.

## Prove it (or break it)

```bash
make redteam      # 23 attacks x 3 designs, same real token; writes docs/redteam/latest.md
make test         # unit, property-based, integration, security
make scenarios    # demonstration scenarios A-M
make verify-ledger
```

The red-team harness compares a **scope-only bank**, an **OAuth + static RAR bank** (stronger than scopes, but deliberately stateless: no sender constraint, online revocation, budgets or approvals, so it is a model of one common design, not of every OAuth deployment) and **KYM**, and includes an attack KYM cannot stop (`in_mandate_malicious`). It runs in the UI at `/proof`. Add an attack that KYM fails and you have improved the project. After `make redteam`, run `make reset-demo` for a clean demo state.

## Run it

Prerequisites: Python ≥ 3.12, [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/), Node 20+ (for the UI). No Docker required.

```bash
make install        # creates .venv and installs pinned backend deps
make install-web    # npm install for the UI
make demo           # migrates + seeds synthetic data, starts API :8000 and UI :3000
```

* API docs (OpenAPI/Swagger): http://127.0.0.1:8000/docs — static copy in [docs/specifications/openapi.json](docs/specifications/openapi.json)
* UI: http://localhost:3000
* Everything else: `make test`, `make scenarios`, `make verify-ledger`, `make benchmark`, `make reset-demo`, `make lint` (see `make help`).
* Docker: `docker compose up --build` (PostgreSQL 16 + API + UI, localhost-bound, demo secrets from `.env.example`). **Verified end to end on 2026-11-27**: the stack built and started, scenarios A–M passed through the containerised API on PostgreSQL 16, the red-team run gave 0/10, 3/10 and 22/22, and the web container proxied the API. Details in [docs/deployment.md](docs/deployment.md).

| `customer_003` Priya Nair, `customer_004` Jordan Lee | authorized signatories of Northwind Supply Inc. (`business_001`) | business treasury / separation of duties |

## Test evidence (recorded from actual runs)

| Suite | Result |
|---|---|
| `make test` — unit, property-based (Hypothesis), integration, security, red-team regression, docs-consistency | **237 passed, 0 failed, 1 skipped** (the PostgreSQL multi-process test runs only when `KYM_TEST_PG_URL` is set; it was run separately); line + branch coverage **82%** (`make coverage`, [how to read it](docs/testing.md)) |
| `make scenarios` — scenarios A–M against the real engine (SQLite), run three times in a row on one database | **13/13 passed each time**; `make verify-ledger` afterwards: 767 events, 8 checkpoints, chain intact |
| Same 13 scenarios + Alembic migration against **PostgreSQL 14** and, through `docker compose`, **PostgreSQL 16** | **13/13 passed** on both |
| `ruff check apps tests` | clean |
| `make redteam` (23 attacks, 3 designs) | scope-only 0/10, OAuth + static RAR 3/10, **KYM 22/22** applicable blocked (10/10 on the same ten attacks the baselines can model); 1 documented honest gap; 0 harness errors ([results](docs/redteam/latest.md)) |
| Web: `tsc`, `eslint`, `next build`, Playwright (Chromium, live API) | clean; **30 passed, 0 failed** ([apps/web/README.md](apps/web/README.md)) |
| `make benchmark` (single process, SQLite, in-process ASGI client) | PDP pure evaluation p50 0.076 ms / p95 0.088 ms / p99 0.135 ms (n=20 000); full gateway payment p50 18.9 ms / p95 24.7 ms / p99 37.0 ms (n=300). Raw output: [docs/benchmarks/latest.json](docs/benchmarks/latest.json) |


## Standards: implemented vs. simulated vs. mapped

Full matrix with sources and "interoperability tested?" (it is **No** everywhere): [docs/research/standards-mapping.md](docs/research/standards-mapping.md), machine-readable [standards/standards.json](standards/standards.json), shown in the UI at `/standards`.

* **Implemented (sandbox quality, using maintained libraries):** JWT/JWS signing & verification (PyJWT, ES256), PKCE S256, RFC 9396 `authorization_details` (proposed type `kym_financial_mandate`), RFC 9449 DPoP proof validation, RFC 7662 introspection, RFC 7009 revocation, RFC 8707 audience check, RFC 8785 JCS (`rfc8785`), RDF/Turtle/JSON-LD (rdflib), SHACL (pySHACL), SPARQL (rdflib, read-only guard), PROV-O and ODRL terms reuse, Ed25519 signatures (`cryptography`).
* **Simulated / simplified:** RFC 9126 PAR, RFC 8693 token exchange, OIDC `id_token`, customer authentication and approval (simulated session — **not** passkeys), agent attestation, KYC, KYT, sanctions screening, payment rails.
* **Conceptually mapped only:** mTLS (RFC 8705), FAPI 2.0, OpenID Shared Signals/CAEP, FDX, AP2 ([mapping](docs/research/ap2-mapping.md)), Visa/Mastercard agentic commerce, ACP, x402, A2A, SPIFFE/SPIRE, OPA/Cedar (not used — a typed Python engine is used).
* **Experimental KYM proposals (not standards):** ontology v1, KYM-CNL, `kym_financial_mandate` RAR type, `https://example.org/kym/*` JWT claims, the evidence ledger design.

## Security limitations (read before drawing conclusions)

* Demo sessions have no authentication; demo keys (ledger, decision, witness, customer consent, agent, authorization server) are plain files under `.kym-data/keys` (mode 0600). Production: HSM/KMS, WORM storage, RFC 3161 timestamping, independent witnesses, SPIFFE/SPIRE, passkeys, mTLS, a FAPI-certified authorization server.
* The ledger is **tamper-evident, not tamper-proof**: whoever can replace the database *and* the keys can rewrite history. The demo adds signed checkpoints, an independent witness key and locally exported checkpoint files to show stronger detection (Scenario L).
* Budget atomicity relies on a global write lock: an in-process lock plus a database-level lock (`BEGIN IMMEDIATE` on SQLite, an advisory lock on PostgreSQL). `make concurrency` races four OS processes for one budget and passed on SQLite and PostgreSQL 16 (without the lock, PostgreSQL runs crashed on the ledger sequence). It is a throughput ceiling, tested at four processes, not at load or across nodes.
* Scenario runs call `demo.prepare_isolated_state()` (demo/test only): it starts a fresh *synthetic risk window* and tops up balances with a balanced `DEMO_TOPUP` double-entry pair, so repeated runs are independent. It never touches the enforcement path.
* Within-mandate mistakes (e.g. paying CAD 90 instead of CAD 9) cannot be detected by mandate enforcement alone (Scenario D).
* A valid signature proves integrity and key control, **not** legally effective consent.

Details: [threat model](docs/threat-model/threat-model.md), [gap analysis](docs/specifications/production-readiness-gap-analysis.md), [regulatory mapping](docs/regulatory-mapping/README.md).

The repository layout deliberately omits empty placeholder services (`services/*`, `scenarios/*` directories): logical components live in one modular monolith with explicit module boundaries ([ADR-0001](docs/adr/0001-modular-monolith.md)).

Questions, corrections, critiques, or a wish to review the design: **email me at [clas.paul@gmail.com](mailto:clas.paul@gmail.com)**, or open a [GitHub issue](https://github.com/PaulClas/Know-The-Mandate/issues) for anything that others may benefit from. Security reports: [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md).

**About the author.** I am Paul Clas, a **machine learning developer**. I built KYM as an independent exploration of how banks might govern the authority they hand to AI agents. I am not a bank, payments-security, cryptography or legal professional, which is why the project publishes its [risks](docs/risk/risk-register.md), [open findings](docs/security/security-review.md) and [call for external review](docs/security/external-review.md) rather than asking you to trust it. Expert criticism is the most useful thing you can send me. Media and citation notes: [media guide](docs/media-guide.md).

## Contributing

Issues and pull requests are welcome, especially **new attacks KYM fails** and corrections to the disclosures. Read [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) and the [Code of Conduct](CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md). The invariants in [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md) apply to humans and coding assistants alike.

## Security policy

Please report vulnerabilities privately; see [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md). KYM is a synthetic-data demo with sandbox security, so the [known limitations](docs/security/security-review.md) are not vulnerabilities, but novel bypasses of the mandate check are very welcome.

See [CITATION.cff](CITATION.cff) (GitHub shows a "Cite this repository" button) and [codemeta.json](codemeta.json). KYM is an experimental proposal, not a standard.

<!-- source: docs/faq.md -->

# KYM frequently asked questions

Answers lead with the direct answer. Last reviewed 2026-11-26. KYM is an experimental, synthetic-data proof of concept; nothing here is legal or compliance advice.

## What is KYM?
**KYM (Know Your Mandate) is an experimental framework that lets a bank represent, enforce and prove the financial authority a customer has delegated to an AI agent.** The customer's authority is captured as a *mandate*: who may act, on which accounts, for what purpose, with which limits and expiry, whether it can be delegated, and which actions need a human. A deterministic policy engine checks the mandate on every request, and a signed evidence ledger records what happened.

## What problem does KYM solve?
**It closes the gap between "this client holds a valid token" and "the customer actually authorized this specific action".** KYC identifies the customer, authentication verifies the caller, OAuth grants API access, KYA identifies the agent, KYT scores transactions. None records the delegated authority itself. Without it, a bank cannot easily answer who authorized what, within which limits, and whether those limits were honoured.

## How is KYM different from OAuth and OAuth Rich Authorization Requests (RAR)?
**OAuth/RAR is the carrier; KYM supplies the state and the decision.** RAR (RFC 9396) can express account, beneficiary and maximum amount inside a token, and KYM uses it. But a static grant cannot track cumulative budgets, instant mandate revocation, single-use approvals or delegation lineage. In KYM's red-team comparison, a stateless design with scopes plus static RAR stopped 3 of the 10 attacks it can model; KYM blocked all 10 of those and 22 of 22 applicable attacks overall (and documents one it cannot stop). The baseline is deliberately stateless, so this shows what needs state, not that no other design could add it. See [philosophy](philosophy/README.md#1-oauth-with-rich-authorization-requests-already-does-this).

## Does a valid access token authorize a payment in KYM?
**No.** A valid token is only technical permission. Scenario C demonstrates it: the token passes OAuth verification (including `payments.initiate`), the mandate does not permit the beneficiary, and the payment is denied.

## Can KYM stop an AI agent from making mistakes or being prompt-injected?
**It limits the damage; it does not prevent the mistake.** Anything outside the mandate is denied no matter why the agent asked (hallucination, injection, compromise). Anything *inside* the mandate is allowed, and mandate enforcement cannot tell a wrong-but-permitted payment from a right one. This is the documented honest gap (`in_mandate_malicious`).

## Is KYM a standard? Is it compliant or certified?
**No.** The vocabulary (`https://example.org/kym/v1#`), the controlled language (KYM-CNL), the `kym_financial_mandate` authorization-details type and the `https://example.org/kym/*` token claims are experimental proposals. The demo claims no compliance, certification or conformance with any law or standard.

## Which standards does it use, and which are only mapped?
**Implemented in a sandbox using maintained libraries:** JWT/JWS (ES256), PKCE, RFC 9396 RAR validation, RFC 9449 DPoP proof validation, introspection, revocation, RFC 8785 canonical JSON, RDF/JSON-LD, SHACL, SPARQL, Ed25519 signatures. **Simplified/simulated:** PAR, token exchange, OIDC, customer authentication, attestation, KYC/KYT/sanctions. **Mapped only:** mTLS, FAPI 2.0, FDX, AP2, Visa/Mastercard, ACP, x402, A2A, SPIFFE/SPIRE, OPA/Cedar. No interoperability has been tested. Details: [standards matrix](research/standards-mapping.md).

## How does KYM relate to Google's AP2, MCP and A2A?
**They are complementary layers, not substitutes.** AP2 concerns agent-driven commerce artifacts (user-approved mandates, checkout and payment proofs); KYM adds the bank-side authority decision and evidence. MCP and A2A are transport/discovery protocols: tool discovery is not permission, and every MCP-shaped call in KYM still passes the same enforcement point. AP2 mapping is conceptual only: [ap2-mapping.md](research/ap2-mapping.md).

## Why not just use Open Policy Agent (OPA) or Cedar?
**You can; KYM chose a typed Python engine for determinism, explanation and replay in one language.** The decision is a pure function of a stored JSON snapshot, which makes a stored decision replayable by re-running the current engine on its snapshot (past engine versions are not archived; see O-22). OPA/Cedar are valid production choices; the snapshot format is the integration seam ([ADR-0002](adr/0002-deterministic-pdp-no-opa.md)).

## Is the ontology used to make authorization decisions?
**No.** OWL reasoning is open-world; money needs deny-by-default. The ontology and SHACL validate mandates when they are created and support explanation and SPARQL queries. The runtime decision uses a compiled policy ([ADR-0003](adr/0003-ontology-not-in-the-decision-path.md)).

## How does revocation work?
**The mandate's lifecycle state is checked on every request, independent of the token.** Revoking a mandate immediately denies later requests even with an unexpired token, cascades to delegated child mandates, and cancels pending approvals and reservations. It does not reverse payments already executed.

## What is the evidence ledger, and is it a blockchain?
**It is a signed, hash-chained, append-only event log with signed checkpoints; it is not a blockchain.** Events use RFC 8785 canonical JSON, SHA-256 and Ed25519. It is tamper-*evident*: someone who replaces the database, the signing keys and exported checkpoints can rewrite history. Production alternatives: HSM, WORM storage, RFC 3161 timestamps, external witnesses.

## Does KYM decide who is legally liable?
**No.** It attributes who did what and which party controlled which system. It distinguishes factual responsibility, contractual responsibility, potential legal liability and final adjudicated liability, and decides none of the last three. A valid signature shows integrity and key control, not legally effective consent.

## Is it ready for production?
**No.** See the [production readiness gap analysis](specifications/production-readiness-gap-analysis.md), the [security review](security/security-review.md) (24 findings fixed, 22 open or accepted) and the [risk register](risk/risk-register.md). Key gaps: no real authentication, plaintext keys, single-process locking, no external audit, sandbox OAuth.

## What are the biggest risks of KYM?
**Approval fatigue, customers misreading mandates, overly broad mandates, coverage gaps when payments bypass the bank, in-mandate harm, insider abuse, and standards absorbing the idea.** Full list with likelihood and impact: [risk register](risk/risk-register.md).

## When should I not use KYM?
**When agents only read data, when a single static per-transaction cap suffices, or when you cannot run a highly available enforcement point.** See [risk register §E](risk/risk-register.md#e-when-you-should-not-use-kym).

## How can I verify the claims myself?
**Run `make redteam`.** It executes 23 attacks against three designs with the same real token and writes [docs/redteam/latest.md](redteam/latest.md). Also `make test` (208 tests incl. property-based), `make scenarios` (13 demonstration scenarios A–M), and `make verify-ledger`.

## How do I run it?
`make install && make install-web && make demo`; API docs at http://127.0.0.1:8000/docs, UI at http://localhost:3000. Demo users and details: [README](../README.md#run-it).

## Who made KYM, and how do I ask a question?

KYM is an independent project by Paul Clas, a machine learning developer; he is not a bank, payments-security, cryptography or legal professional, which is why the project discloses its [risks](risk/risk-register.md) and [open findings](security/security-review.md) and invites [external review](security/external-review.md). Questions, critiques and review offers: clas.paul@gmail.com or a [GitHub issue](https://github.com/PaulClas/Know-The-Mandate/issues). Reporting a vulnerability: [SECURITY.md](../SECURITY.md).

## Has KYM been independently audited?

No. All evidence is self-assessed, plus one AI-assisted hostile review whose findings were fixed. See [external review status](security/external-review.md) and the [media guide](media-guide.md) for what may be claimed.


---

<!-- source: docs/glossary.md -->

# KYM glossary

**Mandate.** A bank-validated, customer-approved, immutable-per-version statement of delegated financial authority: principal, mandatary (agent), purpose, permissions with constraints, prohibitions, aggregate limits, approval obligations, delegation rules, validity and jurisdictions. Lifecycle status is stored separately.

**Mandatary.** The agent (software identity) to which authority is delegated. In KYM it is not a legal person; the responsible operator is a separate legal entity.

**Principal.** The customer (individual or business) who grants the mandate and must control the resources concerned.

**Delegated authority.** What the customer actually allowed, as opposed to *identity* (who) and *technical permission* (what a token can call).

**Effective authority.** The intersection of customer authority, agent capabilities, OAuth authorization, the active mandate, every parent mandate, bank policy, risk controls and operational restrictions. It can never exceed the narrowest boundary.

**Policy Decision Point (PDP).** The pure deterministic function that returns `ALLOW`, `DENY`, `REQUIRE_HUMAN_APPROVAL` or `REFER_TO_RISK_REVIEW` with reason codes and a check-by-check trace.

**Policy Enforcement Point (PEP).** The gateway through which every financial operation passes.

**Decision certificate.** A server-signed, short-lived, single-use record of an `ALLOW` decision bound to the SHA-256 of the exact operation. The payment engine refuses to execute without it.

**Operation hash.** SHA-256 of the canonical operation (account, beneficiary, amount, currency, purpose, reference) plus mandate id/version, principal and agent. Approvals and decisions bind to it.

**Attenuation.** The rule that delegation can only narrow authority: a child mandate can never expand actions, resources, limits, beneficiaries, validity, delegation depth or geography.

**Cascading revocation.** Revoking a parent mandate makes all delegated children unusable immediately.

**Mandate-bound credential.** A DPoP-bound JWT access token that references the mandate id, version and digest, carries RFC 9396 `authorization_details` and an `act` claim for the agent.

**Rich Authorization Requests (RAR, RFC 9396).** OAuth extension for structured `authorization_details`. KYM's proposed type is `kym_financial_mandate`.

**DPoP (RFC 9449).** Sender-constraining of tokens with a proof of possession of a private key, so a stolen token cannot be replayed from elsewhere.

**KYM-CNL.** KYM Controlled Natural Language: a small controlled language (Lark grammar) inspired by the principles of ASD-STE100 that compiles deterministically into a mandate. No ASD-STE100 compliance is claimed.

**KYM Evidence Ledger.** Append-only, hash-chained, Ed25519-signed log of the exercise of authority, with signed checkpoints. Distinct from the double-entry accounting ledger, which records movement of money.

**Checkpoint.** A signed statement of the ledger head (sequence and hash) by the ledger key and an independent witness key, exported outside the database.

**Pinned keys.** Trusted public keys obtained out of band by the verifier. Verifying a package against keys embedded in the package proves only internal consistency.

**Human approval.** A bank-controlled, single-use, expiring approval bound to the exact operation hash, requiring distinct signatories when the mandate says so.

**Know Your Agent (KYA).** Registry and attestation of AI agents as non-human identities, separating agent-declared metadata from bank-verified facts.

**Know Your Transaction (KYT).** Transaction risk assessment. In KYM it is synthetic and separate from mandate authorization.

**Honest gap.** An attack KYM does not stop: payments that stay inside the mandate (`in_mandate_malicious`).

**Baseline (red-team).** Deliberately simple models used for comparison: *scope-only* and *OAuth + static RAR*.


---

<!-- source: docs/philosophy/README.md -->

# The philosophy of KYM, and why it stands against its critics

> **The agent proposes. The mandate authorizes. The bank enforces. The ledger remembers.**

## The problem in one paragraph

Software that can act is not new. What is new is *software with open-ended intent*: an AI agent can decide what to do next. Existing financial controls answer who the customer is (KYC), whether the caller is who it claims to be (authentication), what API a client may call (OAuth), and whether a transaction looks risky (KYT). **None of them records, as a checkable object, what authority a human actually handed to this software.** When something goes wrong, nobody can reconstruct who granted what, under which limits, and whether the bank respected it. KYM's thesis: *delegated financial authority deserves to be a first-class, governed object with a lifecycle.*

## Principles

1. **Authority is not identity, and not permission.** Four things are kept apart: identity, technical permission (a token), delegated authority (a mandate), execution (money moved). A valid token never implies an authorized operation.
2. **Separation of powers.** The agent *proposes* and cannot decide. The mandate *authorizes* and cannot execute. The bank *enforces* and cannot invent authority. The ledger *remembers* and cannot be edited silently. No component can authorize its own action.
3. **Enforce the observable, not the intention.** The bank cannot know whether an agent hallucinated, was injected or was compromised, and does not need to. It checks amounts, beneficiaries, budgets, time, state. This makes enforcement independent of the model.
4. **Deny by default; closed world at runtime.** Ontologies reason under an open world (absence ≠ falsity). Money cannot. Missing authority means denial; semantic technology is used for meaning and validation, never for the decision.
5. **Authority only attenuates.** Delegation can narrow, never widen (capability-security lineage: least privilege, attenuation). A child can never exceed its parent, and revoking a parent disables the children.
6. **Evidence over trust.** Claims should be checkable by someone who does not trust the bank: signed, hash-chained, replayable against the current engine, offline-verifiable (with keys pinned out of band; the verifier also binds the displayed transaction to the signed events). Evidence shows *who did what and under which version*; **it does not decide liability.**
7. **Humans decide exceptions, about exact things.** Approval is bound to the exact operation, single use, expiring, by distinct people where required. One-time approval never expands the mandate.
8. **Extend standards; do not replace them.** OAuth, DPoP, RAR, JSON-LD, SHACL, PROV-O, ODRL are reused. KYM-specific parts are labelled *proposed*.
9. **Honesty is a feature.** Simulated things say so in the UI and docs. Gaps are published (see the [risk register](../risk/risk-register.md)), including attacks KYM does **not** stop.
10. **Narrow claim, falsifiable proof.** KYM does not claim to make AI safe. It claims one thing (below), and ships code that tries to break it.

## The claim, stated narrowly

> A bank can hold an **independent, stateful, revocable representation of delegated authority**, evaluated deterministically on **every** request, that bounds what an agent can do with the bank's money **regardless of how the agent behaves or what credentials it holds**, and can later **prove** what happened.

Everything else (ontology, CNL, delegation graphs, dashboards) serves or illustrates that claim.

## Claims and how to falsify them

| Claim | How to falsify it | Proof in repo |
|---|---|---|
| A valid token cannot move money outside the mandate | Make a payment to a non-permitted beneficiary with a valid token succeed | Scenario C; `redteam: beneficiary_swap`; `tests/integration/test_enforcement.py` |
| Cumulative limits hold under concurrency | Exceed the monthly budget with parallel requests | Scenario H; `redteam: budget_race`; 8-thread test and a 4-process race (`make concurrency`) on SQLite and PostgreSQL. Serialization-based, so throughput-limited; multi-node is untested (O-03) |
| Revocation is immediate and cascades | Execute after revocation with an unexpired token, or via a child | Scenario F, G; `redteam: revoked_mandate` |
| A stolen token is useless to another party | Replay a token or DPoP proof from another key | `redteam: stolen_token`, `dpop_replay` |
| Approvals can't be substituted or replayed | Execute a changed payload, or reuse an approval | Scenario J; `redteam: approval_*` |
| A child can't exceed its parent | Create a wider child by any dimension | `tests/unit/test_properties.py` (Hypothesis); Scenario G |
| Evidence tampering is detectable | Alter, delete or re-hash an event without detection | Scenario L; `redteam: ledger_tamper` |
| Decisions can be reconstructed | Fail to reproduce a decision from stored inputs | Scenario M; `tests/integration` replay tests |
| KYM is more than OAuth + static RAR | Show a static design stopping the stateful attacks | `redteam` comparison (stateless static RAR 3/10 vs KYM 10/10 on the same attacks, 22/22 overall; the baseline is deliberately stateless) |
| **KYM cannot stop in-mandate misuse** (negative claim) | Show a mandate-level control that does | `redteam: in_mandate_malicious` (honest gap) |

Run `make redteam`. Results are written to [docs/redteam/latest.md](../redteam/latest.md).

## The critics, steelmanned

Each objection is stated at its strongest, answered, and then we say **where the critic is right**.

### 1. "OAuth with Rich Authorization Requests already does this."
*Strongest form:* RFC 9396 lets a token carry exactly which account, beneficiary and maximum amount; FAPI and DPoP exist; this is reinvention.
*Answer:* We agree and use them as the carrier. But RAR is a **grant format**: it is static, evaluated against the token, and has no notion of cumulative budgets, mandate revocation independent of the token, approval binding or delegation lineage. In the proof, a design with scopes + static RAR stops swaps and per-payment limits (3 of 10 applicable attacks) and fails budget drain, races, revocation, stolen tokens and approvals. KYM adds the **state** (budgets, lifecycle, approvals) and the **per-request decision**.
*Critic is right that:* if all you need is a per-payment cap, RAR is enough and KYM is overkill.

### 2. "Banks already have limits, SCA and fraud engines."
*Answer:* Those control instruments and transactions; they do not know that a **delegated software actor** is exercising authority for a **named purpose**, nor can they reconstruct delegation. KYM's risk engine is deliberately separate: authorization and risk are different questions.
*Critic is right that:* KYM must integrate with, not replace, existing controls; its risk engine here is synthetic.

### 3. "Mandates and approvals are consent theatre; people click through."
*Answer:* Approvals are bound to the **exact operation**, single use, and rare by design (budgets and thresholds mean most payments need none). That addresses substitution and replay, not fatigue.
*Critic is right that:* approval fatigue is real and unmeasured here. This is the weakest part of the human-in-the-loop story (risk C-1).

### 4. "The real problem is agents being wrong *inside* their permissions."
*Answer:* Correct, and we ship the attack that shows it (`in_mandate_malicious`). Mandates **bound the blast radius**; they do not verify correctness. Defence layers: tight limits, thresholds, notifications, risk models.
*Critic is right.* KYM must never be sold as preventing in-mandate harm.

### 5. "Ontologies, OWL and SHACL are over-engineering. JSON Schema plus code is enough."
*Answer:* The runtime decision does **not** use the ontology (ADR-0003). It earns its place only for interoperable meaning, validation of mandate graphs, explanation and SPARQL queries across mandates, delegation and evidence (e.g. "which mandates depend on a revoked parent?").
*Critic is right that:* a deployment with no need for shared semantics can drop it and keep everything else.

### 6. "A hash chain is blockchain theatre; logs are fine."
*Answer:* No blockchain is used. Signed hash chains make *silent* edits detectable, and the proof tampers four ways and fails to evade detection. Evidence packages verify offline.
*Critic is right that:* an operator who controls the database, keys and exported checkpoints can rewrite history; real assurance needs WORM storage, timestamping and external witnesses. Also right that an unpinned verifier is fooled (we found and fixed that, F-01).

### 7. "Networks and wallets (AP2, Visa, Mastercard) will own agentic commerce; banks will be bypassed."
*Answer:* The account-holding bank remains the final authority over its own accounts, and AP2-style artifacts map onto KYM concepts (see [AP2 mapping](../research/ap2-mapping.md)). Layers are complementary: merchant-side intent proofs vs. bank-side authority enforcement.
*Critic is right that:* if payments route around the bank's decision, KYM is irrelevant there (risk D-2).

### 8. "LLM guardrails and alignment are the answer."
*Answer:* Guardrails are probabilistic and bypassable; KYM is deterministic and model-independent. They are complementary: guardrails reduce harmful attempts, mandates cap consequences when guardrails fail.
*Critic is right that:* guardrails also address harms KYM does not (misinformation, privacy, in-mandate misuse).

### 9. "Centralized enforcement is a single point of failure and a gatekeeping tool."
*Answer:* Fail-closed is intentional for money. High availability and fair-access policy are engineering and regulatory matters.
*Critic is right.* No HA design exists here, and gatekeeping risk is real (C-5, C-11).

### 10. "'Mandate' has legal meaning; an AI can't be a mandatary."
*Answer:* Agreed, and KYM says so: the AI is not a legal person; the responsible operator is modelled separately; evidence is not a liability finding; nothing claims legal effect.
*Critic is right that:* terminology invites misreading; legal review is required (D-4).

### 11. "This is a self-graded demo."
*Answer:* Yes. The response is to make claims **falsifiable and reproducible** (`make redteam`, public tests, published gaps) and to invite external attack.
*Critic is right.* Until independently tested, KYM is a hypothesis with working code.

### 12. "Too complex for the benefit."
*Answer:* It need not be adopted whole.

## Adoption ladder

| Level | What | Gain | Cost |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | Scopes + consent management | Data access control | Low |
| 1 | + RAR (static account/beneficiary/amount) + DPoP | Stops swaps, over-limit, token theft | Low–Med |
| 2 | + Mandate registry, PDP, budgets, revocation | Stateful limits, instant revocation, approvals | Med |
| 3 | + Evidence ledger, replay, dispute packages | Provable reconstruction | Med–High |
| 4 | + Delegation, ontology/SPARQL, CNL studio | Multi-agent governance, shared semantics | High |

## What would change our mind

* A realistic attack in the red-team harness that a *simpler* design stops and KYM does not.
* Evidence that approvals degrade to rubber-stamping at scale, with no UX fix.
* A standard (RAR + Grant Management + a budget extension) that supplies state, revocation and evidence with less machinery.
* A legal conclusion that such evidence has no value.

If any of these occurs, the right response is to simplify or stop, not to rebrand.


---

<!-- source: docs/risk/risk-register.md -->

# KYM risk register and disclosures

This register covers **everything the authors believe could go wrong with KYM**: attacks, insider abuse, design flaws, legal exposure, adoption failure and ways the idea itself could be wrong or misused. It is written to be read by critics. Technical findings with proofs are in [../security/security-review.md](../security/security-review.md).

Scoring is qualitative (L = low, M = medium, H = high), by the authors, **before external review**. "Residual" is the risk left after the described mitigation *as implemented in this repository*.

## A. Disclosures up front

1. **Experimental, synthetic, self-assessed.** No real money, customers or regulators were involved. No external security audit, penetration test, formal verification or production pilot has occurred.
2. **Not compliant, certified or legal advice.** Regulatory mappings are research aids; several items are marked unverified.
3. **Sandbox security mechanisms.** The OAuth server is a sandbox adapter; customer authentication and consent are simulated; keys are files.
4. **KYM does not make agents safe.** It limits what an agent can *do with the bank's money*. It does not make the agent correct, honest or aligned.
5. **KYM can be misused.** A bank could use broad "consent receipts" to shift blame to customers (see C-9).
6. **The namespace is a placeholder** (`https://example.org/kym/v1#`), not a governed vocabulary.
7. **The red-team baselines are simple models** of common designs. They demonstrate specific gaps; they are not a market comparison.

## B. Security and hacking risks

| ID | Risk | L | I | Mitigation in repo | Residual |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| S-1 | Stolen or shared access token | M | H | DPoP sender-constraint, short TTL, per-request mandate checks | **L–M**: key theft from the agent host still works within the mandate |
| S-2 | Compromised agent runtime or key | M | H | Blast radius bounded by amounts, beneficiaries, budget, expiry, approvals | **M**: attacker can spend the whole budget at allowed beneficiaries |
| S-3 | Prompt injection / hallucination | H | M | Deterministic enforcement; injected content cannot widen authority | **M**: in-mandate harm is undetectable by design (proof `in_mandate_malicious`) |
| S-4 | Operator/insider abuse (reverse payments, clear reviews, suspend agents, read evidence) | M | H | Role checks, evidence events for actions | **H**: no maker–checker, no admin-read logging (O-04, O-19) |
| S-5 | Host or database compromise | M | H | Signed decisions, hash chain, checkpoints | **H**: plaintext keys, single trust domain (O-02, O-16) |
| S-6 | Ledger rewriting by an attacker who owns DB and keys | L | H | Signed checkpoints with witness key, exported checkpoint files | **M–H**: needs WORM/external witness (O-07) |
| S-7 | Forged or misleading evidence package | M | H | Pinned-key verification (fixed F-01) | **L** if verifiers pin keys; **H** if they trust embedded keys |
| S-8 | Denial of service (write lock, ledger flood, SPARQL, auth CPU) | M | M | Rate limits, caps, subprocess sandbox, auth outside lock | **M**: single-process design (O-03, O-10) |
| S-9 | Reconnaissance via denial reasons | H | L–M | None (disclosed) | **M** (O-15) |
| S-10 | Replay of approvals/proofs | L | M | Operation-hash binding, single use, jti cache | **L**; DPoP nonce absent (O-06) |
| S-11 | Supply-chain compromise | M | H | Few well-known libraries, pinned | **M** (O-13) |
| S-12 | Web-UI token theft (XSS) | L | H | React escaping, no HTML injection paths | **M**: `localStorage` + no CSP (O-14) |
| S-13 | Time-boundary budget errors | L | M | Calendar windows in IANA zones | **M**: limited DST tests (O-20) |
| S-14 | Decision-snapshot manipulation by a compromised gateway | L | H | Replay detects non-determinism | **M**: garbage-in not detectable (O-17) |
| S-15 | Deceptive or erroneous consent rendering | M | H | Digest-bound receipt, EN/FR summaries, tests on content | **M–H** (O-18) |

## C. Design flaws and "ways KYM could fail as an idea"

| ID | Risk | L | I | Assessment |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| C-1 | **Approval fatigue / consent theatre.** Frequent prompts train humans to click Approve. | H | H | Mitigated only partially by thresholds, exact-operation binding and limits that keep approvals rare. Approval rate is measured (`human_approval_rate` metric) but **no user study exists**. This is probably the biggest practical threat to the human-in-the-loop claim. |
| C-2 | **Customers misunderstand mandates.** The summary says X, the customer thinks Y; CNL and ontologies are not consumer language. | H | H | EN/FR plain summaries and ambiguity detection help; unvalidated with real users. |
| C-3 | **Mandate over-breadth.** Customers/agents/banks default to broad mandates; the control degrades to "yes". | M | H | Bank policy caps (per-payment cap, validity, forbidden actions) and mandatory aggregate limits exist; policy tuning is unproven. |
| C-4 | **False sense of security.** Teams relax other controls because "there is a mandate". | M | M | Documentation stresses defence in depth; cannot be enforced technically. |
| C-5 | **Fail-closed availability.** If the PDP, ledger or registry is down, agent payments stop. | M | M | Deliberate trade-off; no HA design exists. |
| C-6 | **Operational complexity and cost.** Ontology + SHACL + CNL + OAuth + ledger + registry is a lot to operate. | H | M | Mitigated by the adoption ladder in [philosophy](../philosophy/README.md#adoption-ladder): the ontology is optional (ADR-0003). |
| C-7 | **Performance and hot-row contention** (per-request budget aggregation across delegation chains). | M | M | Measured in-process (PDP 0.08 ms; gateway payment p50 19 ms single-process); not load-tested at scale. |
| C-8 | **Policy errors.** A wrong bank policy or wrong CNL compile silently authorizes the wrong thing. | M | H | Deterministic compile, SHACL + bank checks, replay; correctness of the *policy* is human. |
| C-9 | **Blame shifting / dark patterns.** Consent receipts could be used to claim the customer "authorized" harm. | M | H | Receipts carry assurance level and a legal note; bank caps limit exposure; but incentives are outside software. Regulators and law, not code, must allocate liability. |
| C-10 | **Privacy tension.** Immutable logs vs. erasure rights; hashes of low-entropy fields are guessable. | M | M | Payload store is erasable; chain commits to digests. Snapshots are not minimised (O-08). |
| C-11 | **Concentrated power.** KYM strengthens the bank's role as gatekeeper for agent access and could be used anti-competitively against third-party agents. | M | M | Not addressable in code; relevant to open-banking policy. |

## D. Strategic and "downfall" risks

| ID | Risk | L | I | Assessment |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| D-1 | **Standards absorb or bypass it.** OAuth RAR/Grant Management, AP2, networks' agent-payment schemes could cover the same ground, leaving KYM as an orphan vocabulary. | M | H | KYM is designed as a layer *on* RAR/DPoP and maps AP2; its own namespace is the least durable part. If the standards win, the architecture lessons survive, the vocabulary may not. |
| D-2 | **Coverage gap.** Agentic commerce may route authority through merchants, wallets or networks that never ask the account-holding bank. KYM governs only the bank's own rails. | M | H | Real limit on relevance. |
| D-3 | **Adoption chicken-and-egg.** Banks adopt only if agents exist; agents adopt only if banks offer it. | H | H | Unaddressed. |
| D-4 | **Legal non-recognition.** Courts or regulators may not treat the evidence or mandate semantics as meaningful; "mandate" has defined meaning in some jurisdictions (e.g. Québec). The AI is not a legal person; this is stated everywhere. | M | M–H | Not resolved by technology. |
| D-5 | **Unproven.** One implementation, authored and attacked by the same team, no pilot. | H | H | Biggest strategic risk. The proof harness makes claims *falsifiable*; external replication is invited. |
| D-6 | **Governance vacuum.** No steward for the vocabulary, policy catalogue or reference implementation. | H | M | Open. |

## E. When you should NOT use KYM

* Your agents only **read** data and never initiate money movement: scopes plus consent management are enough.
* You need only a single per-transaction cap and nothing stateful: OAuth with RAR (or card-network limits) is simpler (the proof shows static RAR stops swaps and over-limit payments).
* You cannot operate a low-latency, highly available enforcement point on the bank's critical path.
* You expect it to prevent harm from within-mandate mistakes or malicious-but-permitted requests.

## F. Pre-mortem: the most likely story of failure

*Banks built it and customers ignored the summaries; most approvals were clicked through; mandates were broad because narrow ones were annoying; incidents occurred inside mandates; the bank's lawyers used the receipts to argue consent; payment networks shipped their own agent credentials and banks had no say.* None of that is prevented by this code. The mitigations are product design, regulation and ecosystem politics, which is why the repository labels itself a proof of concept for a *control-plane idea*, not a solution to agentic risk.

## G. How to challenge this register

Run `make redteam`, read [docs/redteam/latest.md](../redteam/latest.md), and add attacks to `apps/api/kym/redteam.py`. Pull requests that add a failing attack are more valuable than praise.


---

<!-- source: docs/security/security-review.md -->

# KYM security review and cybersecurity-framework assessment

**Scope:** the full repository as of 2026-11-26 (backend `apps/api/kym`, web `apps/web`, infrastructure files). **Type:** self-assessment by the authors of the code, with executable regression proofs. **This is not an independent penetration test, audit or certification.** Self-review is biased toward finding what the reviewer already thought of; external review is listed as required work.

Machine-checkable evidence: `make redteam` (23 attacks, 3 designs), `tests/security/`, `tests/integration/`. Generated results: [docs/redteam/latest.md](../redteam/latest.md).

## 1. Method

1. Read every endpoint and trust boundary against the STRIDE model in [threat-model.md](../threat-model/threat-model.md).
2. Map the implementation to OWASP API Security Top 10 (2023), NIST CSF 2.0 functions and agent-specific risks.
3. Attack it: each suspected weakness got a reproducing test *before* the fix, then a regression test after (`redteam.py`).
4. Record what was **fixed**, what is **accepted** and what is **open**. Nothing is hidden by wording.

Framework sources checked on 2026-11-26 against the official publications: OWASP API Security Top 10 2023 (category names, api-security.owasp.org); OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025 (LLM01-LLM10 names, genai.owasp.org/llm-top-10); OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications 2026 (ASI01-ASI10 names, genai.owasp.org/top-10-for-agentic-applications-2026); NIST CSF 2.0 categories `PR.AA` (Identity Management, Authentication, and Access Control; `PR.AA-05` covers access permissions and authorizations defined in policy, managed, enforced and reviewed) and `DE.CM` (Continuous Monitoring), read from NIST's published CSF 2.0 reference data. Only names and identifiers were checked; the *mapping* of KYM behaviour to each item is the authors' indicative judgement, not an assessment by OWASP or NIST.

## 2. Findings register

Severity is the authors' judgement *in a deployed setting*, not in the local demo. "Fixed" means a regression test exists.

### Fixed during this review

| ID | Finding | Sev. | Fix | Proof |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| F-01 | **Evidence verifier trusted public keys embedded in the package.** A forger who re-signs every event with their own key and swaps the embedded key passed verification. `POST /api/evidence/verify` was exposed to this. | High | `verify_package(trusted_keys=…)`; endpoint pins the bank's key registry; report states `key_trust`; CLI `kym verify-package --keys`. | `redteam: forged_evidence_package` (unpinned verifier is fooled, pinned is not) |
| F-02 | **Unauthenticated ledger flooding.** Every request with a bad token appended a signed `TOKEN_REJECTED` event and held the write lock. | High | Per-IP rate limit; global cap on rejection events (excess counted in metrics, not written). | `redteam: unauth_flood` (300 junk requests → ≤ 60 events, ledger intact) |
| F-03 | **scrypt client authentication ran inside the global write lock**, so unauthenticated bad credentials stalled all writers. | High | Authenticate in a read context first; failed-auth lockout. | `redteam: client_auth_bruteforce` |
| F-04 | **SPARQL timeout could not kill the worker thread.** A hostile aggregate query could saturate the pool (DoS). | Med | Queries run in a child process with `RLIMIT_CPU`/`RLIMIT_AS`, killed on timeout. | `redteam: sparql_dos` |
| F-05 | **Path traversal:** `agent_id` became part of a key file name. | Med | Strict `^agent_[a-z0-9_]{2,60}$` validation at the sink and the API. | `redteam: path_traversal` |
| F-06 | **Constant session-signing secret** shipped in source and Compose → anyone could forge an admin session if the API was reachable. | High (if exposed) | Random per-install secret in `keys/session-secret`; legacy constant rejected. | `redteam: session_forgery` |
| F-07 | **No fail-closed switch** for no-password sessions and destructive reset. | Med | `KYM_ENV` (default `demo`); any other value disables login, API sessions, reset and red-team runs. | `redteam: production_fail_closed` |
| F-08 | No rate limiting or lockout on OAuth/bank endpoints. | Med | Sliding-window limiter, failed-auth lockout (`429`). | `test_rate_limit_applies…` |
| F-09 | No security headers or body-size cap. | Low | `nosniff`, `X-Frame-Options`, CSP `default-src 'none'`, `no-store`, 1 MB body cap. | `test_security_headers_and_body_limit` |
| F-10 | Unvalidated identifiers flowed into RDF IRIs (graph/serialization injection). | Low–Med | `ID_RE` validation on resources, beneficiaries, merchants, accounts. | schema tests |
| F-11 | Oversized or float amounts could overflow the database layer (500). | Low | `MAX_MINOR = 10^15`, integer-only validation. | `redteam: malformed_input` |
| F-12 | Non-object JSON bodies caused 500s. | Low | `_json_obj` validation, MCP adapter guards. | `redteam: malformed_input` |
| F-13 | DPoP replay cache grew without bound. | Low–Med | Entries older than 300 s deleted on insert. | code + DPoP tests |
| F-14 | Transfer to the same account, or to a destination in a different currency, was accepted (integrity). | Med | Rejected at normalization; engine refuses currency-mismatched or closed destination. | engine path |
| F-15 | Unbounded idempotency-key length. | Low | 1–128 characters. | gateway |
| F-16 | Deleting the whole ledger passed checkpoint verification: the truncation test required a non-empty event list (found by an independent review). | High | An empty chain is truncation whenever a signed checkpoint commits to later events. | `test_review_findings` |
| F-17 | Counterparty type came from the request: a beneficiary could be addressed as a merchant and judged by merchant-category rules. | Med–High | Type must match the payee registry (400 otherwise). | `test_review_findings` |
| F-18 | Spend was bucketed by creation time, so a payment held for approval across midnight or month end escaped the later window. | Med | Budgets are counted when money moves: new `transactions.executed_at` column (migration `0002`, backfilled). | `test_review_findings` |
| F-19 | A token's own, narrower `authorization_details` (amount, accounts, beneficiaries) were ignored; only scopes and the mandate were checked. | Med | The PDP also requires the request to fit the token's grant (judged last, so a mandate denial stays the primary reason). | `test_review_findings` |
| F-20 | RFC 8693-style token exchange did not require the DPoP key to be the agent's registered key. | Med | Same key pinning as the authorization-code grant. | `test_review_findings` |
| F-21 | `verify_package` trusted unsigned display fields and a supplied replay flag; a package could show a transaction its signed events did not support. | High | Displayed amount, account, payee, op hash, decision and EXECUTED status are bound to signed ledger payloads; replay is recomputed locally. | `test_review_findings` |
| F-22 | A leaked parent token plus the child's credentials was enough to exchange for a child token (no proof of possession of the subject token). | Med | The parent must co-sign the exchange (`subject_dpop`, bound to the subject token by `ath` and to its `cnf.jkt`); proofs are single-use. | `test_review_findings` |
| F-23 | **Writers were serialized only inside one process.** With several PostgreSQL workers, concurrent writes collided on the evidence-ledger sequence (observed: `UniqueViolation` on `evidence_events_pkey`) and budget reads could interleave. | High | `db.write()` takes a database-level lock: `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` (SQLite) or a transaction-scoped advisory lock (PostgreSQL). | `scripts/concurrency_check.py`: 4 processes racing one budget on SQLite and PostgreSQL 16 (3/3 runs held the limit; with the lock removed, PostgreSQL runs crashed) |
| F-24 | A decision certificate was not bound to its transaction; identical operations could in principle reuse each other's certificate. | Low–Med | The signed certificate carries `tx_id`; execution refuses a mismatch. The engine also re-derives the operation hash from the stored operation before moving money. | `test_review_findings` |

### Accepted or open (not fixed in this repository)

| ID | Item | Why it matters | Needed |
|---|---|---|---|
| O-01 | **Demo sessions have no authentication.** Anyone who can reach the API can act as admin. | Critical if exposed. Default bind is loopback/Compose localhost. | OIDC + passkeys; never run `KYM_ENV=demo` on a reachable host. |
| O-02 | Keys, agent private keys and agent client secrets are plaintext files; the "agent" runs inside the server process for the demo. | Host compromise = total compromise; agents are not independent. | HSM/KMS; real agents hold their own keys (SPIFFE/SPIRE, hardware-backed). |
| O-03 | One global write lock serializes all mutations (in-process lock plus a database-level lock: `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` / PostgreSQL advisory lock). Cross-process safety is tested; throughput is bounded by serialization. | Throughput ceiling; a slow transaction delays everyone; authenticated agents can contend for the lock. Tested at 4 processes, not at load. | Row-level locks on budget rows, per-principal serialization, a queue. |
| O-04 | **No maker–checker for bank operators.** One admin can suspend agents, reverse payments, clear risk reviews. | Insider risk. | Dual control, privileged-access management, signed operator actions. |
| O-05 | A business mandate can be approved by a **single** signatory (only *payments* can require two). | Weaker than typical corporate-authority rules. | Mandate-level multi-signatory policy. |
| O-06 | No server-issued DPoP nonces (RFC 9449 §8). | Proofs can be pre-generated within the 60 s `iat` window. | Nonce challenge. |
| O-07 | Ledger is tamper-**evident**: whoever replaces DB **and** keys **and** exported checkpoints can rewrite history. | Core limitation of any self-hosted log. | WORM, RFC 3161 timestamps, external witnesses, Merkle log. |
| O-08 | Decision snapshots store customer/mandate data in the database; only event payloads are erasable. | Privacy-law retention vs. erasure tension. | Snapshot minimisation and key-based erasure. |
| O-09 | SPARQL over the registry graph gives admins/investigators all rows (no row-level authorization). | Over-broad internal access. | Per-case scoped graphs. |
| O-10 | Rate limiter is in-process and ignores `X-Forwarded-For`. Behind a proxy, all clients share one bucket. | Mis-sized limits; trivial self-DoS or bypass depending on topology. | Edge/WAF limiter and trusted-proxy configuration. |
| O-11 | Rejection-event sampling (F-02) means a burst's individual rejections are only counted. | Forensic detail lost under attack. | Separate high-volume security log with independent retention. |
| O-12 | Risk engine and ambiguity detector are simple and rule-based; the trust score is gameable. | False negatives; adaptive attackers. | Governed models, red-team the models. |
| O-13 | Dependencies are version-pinned, not hash-locked; no SBOM. Scanning is configured (`pip-audit`, `npm audit`, gitleaks, CodeQL in `.github/workflows/security.yml`; local `pip-audit` and `npm audit` found nothing on 2026-11-27) but the workflows have not yet run on GitHub. | Supply-chain exposure (a listed threat). | Hash-locking, SBOM, SCA, signed releases. |
| O-14 | UI keeps the session token in `localStorage`; the web app sets no CSP. | An XSS would exfiltrate admin sessions. (React escapes output; the only `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` is a constant theme script.) | HttpOnly cookies + CSRF protection + CSP. |
| O-15 | **Denial responses reveal policy structure** (limits, allowed-beneficiary checks) to the calling agent. | An adaptive agent can map limits by probing. | A terse mode for agent-facing errors; detailed reasons only to the bank/customer. |
| O-16 | Gateway, PDP, risk engine and payment engine share one process and trust domain. | A single code-execution bug defeats separation of duties. | Separate processes with mutual authentication; signed decisions already make this possible. |
| O-17 | Decision replay proves the *engine is deterministic* over the stored snapshot, not that the snapshot was complete or honest when built. | A compromised gateway could build misleading inputs. | Independent input attestations; sampling replay by a second implementation. |
| O-18 | **"What you see is what you sign":** the consent summary is generated by the bank; its digest is recorded, but an incorrect or deceptive generator would mislead the customer. | Central to the thesis; the approval is only as good as the rendering. | Independent summary verification, accessibility and usability studies. |
| O-19 | Admin reads of evidence are not themselves logged. | Insider snooping undetected. | Access logging into a separate ledger. |
| O-20 | Time-window logic (day/month in IANA zones) is property-tested across DST transitions, a 30-minute-DST zone, leap years and year ends (`tests/unit/test_time_windows.py`), but not for zones whose DST change falls at local midnight. | Budget miscounts at those boundaries. | Extend the zone list; test against a second implementation. |
| O-21 | No external penetration test, no fuzzing campaign, no formal verification, no real-world pilot. | Unknown unknowns. | All of the above. |
| O-22 | Replay re-runs the **current** engine. Each signed decision now records an engine fingerprint, so a changed engine is reported as `engine_changed` (a warning) rather than as tampering, but past engine versions are not archived, so an old decision cannot be re-run with its original code from this repository alone. | Historical replay is verifiable only while the engine is unchanged. | Tag and archive engine builds by `policy_version`; replay in a pinned container. |

## 3. OWASP API Security Top 10 (2023) mapping

| Risk | KYM status |
|---|---|
| API1 Broken Object Level Authorization | Customer-scoped checks on mandates, transactions, evidence, ledger events (`auth.assert_can_act_for`); test `cross_customer`. Residual: O-09. |
| API2 Broken Authentication | Agent side: confidential clients (scrypt), DPoP, PKCE, short-lived tokens, lockout. Human side: **demo-only, no authentication (O-01)**. |
| API3 Broken Object Property Level Authorization | Response models are hand-built views; `declared` agent metadata can't set `status`; extra mandate fields are rejected (`extra="forbid"`). No generic mass assignment paths found. |
| API4 Unrestricted Resource Consumption | Rate limits, body cap, SPARQL sandbox, ledger-event cap, bounded DPoP cache, `limit` caps. Residual: O-03, O-10. |
| API5 Broken Function Level Authorization | Role dependencies per route (`require_role`); tests assert customers cannot call admin routes and admins cannot approve. Residual: O-04. |
| API6 Unrestricted Access to Sensitive Business Flows | This is KYM's subject: budgets, approvals, idempotency, concurrency tests. |
| API7 SSRF | No server-side fetching of user-supplied URLs; SPARQL `SERVICE`/`FROM` blocked. |
| API8 Security Misconfiguration | Headers, fail-closed `KYM_ENV`, no default secrets, CORS limited to localhost origins. Residual: O-14. |
| API9 Improper Inventory Management | OpenAPI is generated and committed (`docs/specifications/openapi.json`); sandbox, playground and red-team endpoints are labelled and demo-gated. |
| API10 Unsafe Consumption of APIs | No third-party API is consumed. MCP/AP2 adapters are sandbox/mapping only. |

## 4. NIST CSF 2.0 function view (authors' mapping, not an attestation)

| Function | Present | Gaps |
|---|---|---|
| Govern | Documented invariants (`AGENTS.md`), ADRs, risk register, honest labelling | No governance process, no owners, no policy change control |
| Identify | Threat model, agent registry, asset/trust-boundary diagrams | No asset inventory beyond the repo |
| Protect | Deny-by-default PDP, DPoP, scoped access, validation, headers, rate limits | Plaintext keys, no real authentication, O-04/O-16 |
| Detect | Signed evidence ledger, verification endpoint, decision replay, metrics | No alerting, no anomaly detection on operators (O-19) |
| Respond | Revocation with cascade, agent suspension, pending-operation cancellation, dispute reconstruction | No incident-response runbooks or case management |
| Recover | Reproducible seed/reset, migrations | No backup/restore, DR, or tested recovery of the ledger |

## 5. Agent-specific risk view

| Risk | How KYM treats it |
|---|---|
| Prompt injection / excessive agency (OWASP LLM01/LLM06 in the 2025 list) | Capability is bounded by the mandate; injected content cannot widen it (`prompt_injection` proof). It cannot stop injected requests that stay **inside** the mandate (`in_mandate_malicious`). |
| Confused deputy / token sharing | Actor binding (`act`), DPoP key binding, per-request mandate lookup. |
| Compromised agent runtime | Blast radius = the mandate (amounts, beneficiaries, budget, expiry) plus approvals. The agent's own key can still be used by the attacker within those bounds. |
| Non-human-identity sprawl | Registry with status/attestation; no expiry/recertification (open). |
| Malicious tool output / supply chain | Tool outputs are data; no bank decision depends on them. Dependency risks: O-13. |

## 6. Verdict

KYM's **core design claim**, that authority can be represented, evaluated per request, revoked and evidenced independently of tokens, is supported by the executable proofs. Its **implementation** is a well-tested prototype with real vulnerabilities found and fixed in this pass, and a long list of production gaps above. The honest summary: *the architecture is sound enough to be worth external review; the code is not ready to guard money.*


---

<!-- source: docs/specifications/mandate-spec.md -->

# KYM mandate specification (experimental v1.0.0)

Namespace: `https://example.org/kym/v1#` — **experimental placeholder, not a standard**. JSON Schema: [`packages/mandate-schema/mandate.schema.json`](../../packages/mandate-schema/mandate.schema.json) (generated from `apps/api/kym/schemas.py`; a test fails if it drifts). TypeScript mirror: `apps/web/lib/types.ts`.

## Document

Fields follow the project brief. Additions: top-level `currency` (single currency per mandate), `permissions[].constraints.allowed_merchants|allowed_destination_accounts`, `lineage` (child mandates), `obligations.required_approvals`. Rules enforced by the model: integer minor units (no floats), UTC timestamps `YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SSZ`, IANA `budget_timezone`, permit/prohibit conflict rejected, delegation depth 0 when delegation disallowed, unknown fields rejected.

Digest: `sha256:` of the RFC 8785 canonical JSON of the content (`canon.digest`). Lifecycle status, counters and revocation are **not** part of the signed content.

## Action taxonomy (no implicit inheritance)

`ReadFinancialData` (accounts.read, balances.read, transactions.read, accounts.owner.read, data.transmit_external) · `AnalyzeFinancialData` (analysis.*) · `PrepareFinancialOperation` (payments.prepare, transfers.prepare, investments.prepare) · `ExecuteFinancialOperation` (payments.initiate, payments.pay_invoice, purchases.goods, transfers.execute (internal), transfers.external, investments.trade) · `ManageFinancialAuthority` (mandates.request, mandates.delegate, mandates.revoke). Preparing ≠ executing; balance ≠ transactions; internal ≠ external transfer.

## Decisions and reason codes

Decisions: `ALLOW`, `DENY`, `REQUIRE_HUMAN_APPROVAL`, `REFER_TO_RISK_REVIEW`. Base reason codes: AGENT_NOT_VERIFIED, AGENT_SUSPENDED, INVALID_TOKEN, INVALID_ACTOR_BINDING, TOKEN_SCOPE_INSUFFICIENT, MANDATE_NOT_FOUND, MANDATE_EXPIRED, MANDATE_REVOKED, MANDATE_VERSION_MISMATCH, RESOURCE_NOT_AUTHORIZED, ACTION_NOT_AUTHORIZED, PURPOSE_NOT_AUTHORIZED, BENEFICIARY_NOT_AUTHORIZED, CURRENCY_NOT_AUTHORIZED, TRANSACTION_LIMIT_EXCEEDED, DAILY_LIMIT_EXCEEDED, MONTHLY_LIMIT_EXCEEDED, DELEGATION_NOT_ALLOWED, DELEGATION_EXCEEDS_PARENT, HUMAN_APPROVAL_REQUIRED, RISK_THRESHOLD_EXCEEDED.

KYM extensions (documented additions): CUSTOMER_NOT_VERIFIED, ACCOUNT_RESTRICTED, MANDATE_NOT_YET_VALID, MANDATE_SUSPENDED, MERCHANT_NOT_AUTHORIZED, DELEGATION_CYCLE, APPROVAL_INVALID, POLICY_INPUT_UNVERIFIABLE, RISK_REVIEW_REQUIRED.

## Credentials (proposed extensions)

Access token: ES256 JWT with `iss`, `sub` (customer), `aud` (`https://bank.example/api`), `client_id`, `act.sub` (agent; nested for exchanged tokens), `scope`, `jti`, `iat`, `exp` (5 min), `cnf.jkt`, `authorization_details` (RFC 9396, type `kym_financial_mandate`) and the proposed claims `https://example.org/kym/mandate_id|mandate_version|mandate_hash`. These claims and the RAR type are **KYM proposals, not IETF-standardized**.

Illustrative scopes (bank-defined): accounts.read, balances.read, transactions.read, payments.prepare, payments.initiate, transfers.initiate. Scopes cannot express account, beneficiary, amount, cumulative limit, purpose, schedule, delegation depth, approvals or revocation state — those live in the RAR and the server-side mandate (`taxonomy.SCOPE_GAPS`).

## Budgets

Calendar day/month windows are computed in the mandate's `budget_timezone` (wall-clock midnight, DST-safe) and converted to UTC instants. Usage = executed + reserved money-moving transactions whose `mandate_chain` contains the mandate (so a child consumes its own and every ancestor's budget).

## Open-banking API note

`GET /bank/accounts[/{id}[/balances|/transactions]]` resemble FDX-style account/balance/transaction resources (field names are KYM-sandbox, not FDX schemas; FDX conformance is not claimed). `POST /bank/payments`, `/bank/payments/proposals`, `/bank/transfers` and the decision/approval model are KYM sandbox extensions. Data-access and payment-initiation authority are separate: a token for balances.read cannot move money.


---

<!-- source: docs/specifications/production-readiness-gap-analysis.md -->

# Production readiness gap analysis

KYM is a proof of concept. Gaps below are **not** closed in this repository.

| Area | Demo | Needed for production |
|---|---|---|
| Customer authentication & consent | Role sessions without passwords; server-held demo keys; `DEMO_SIMULATED_SESSION` assurance | OIDC with passkeys/WebAuthn, step-up auth, customer-held keys or qualified e-signature where law requires, accessibility and fraud analytics |
| Authorization server | Sandbox adapter on PyJWT/cryptography; no mTLS, refresh, JARM, request objects | FAPI 2.0-certified server (conformance testing), mTLS or DPoP at scale, key rotation, client registration |
| Keys | PEM files in `.kym-data/keys` | HSM/KMS, separation of ledger/decision/consent keys, rotation and revocation, key ceremonies |
| Evidence ledger | Local hash chain + signed checkpoints + file export | WORM storage, RFC 3161 timestamping, Merkle transparency log, external audit witnesses, retention/legal hold, tested restore |
| Concurrency | Single-process lock + DB transactions (SQLite, PostgreSQL 14 single process verified) | Row-level locking/serializable isolation, idempotency stores, multi-node tests, outbox if the ledger becomes a service |
| Isolation | Modular monolith | Separate trust domains for PEP, payment engine and ledger with mutual authentication (mTLS/SPIFFE), network policy |
| Agent identity | Demo attestation signed by a demo key | SPIFFE/SPIRE or cloud workload identity federation, SLSA/in-toto provenance, hardware-backed keys, continuous posture (CAEP/SSF) |
| Risk/KYT/KYC/AML | Synthetic signals and watch list | Licensed screening, model governance, regulator-approved controls, case management for referred items (clearing workflow not implemented) |
| Payments | Simulated double-entry | Real rails, settlement, reconciliation, reversal/chargeback processes |
| Policy lifecycle | Versioned JSON file | Change control, separation of duties, staged rollout, policy-version floors, shadow evaluation |
| Mandate semantics | Single currency per mandate, subset of constraints | Recurring schedules, multi-currency, merchant category handling, revocation of delegated child by parent agent, amendment diffing UX |
| Ops | Metrics in-process (real p50/p95/p99), structured logs minimal | OpenTelemetry export, SLOs, alerting, DR, capacity tests, security testing and pen test, SBOM, hash-locked dependencies |
| Legal/regulatory | Mappings with official URLs; several items unverified (see regulatory README) | Counsel review per jurisdiction; no automated liability determination; privacy impact assessment; French-language review |
| Interoperability | None tested | Conformance suites; AP2/MCP/A2A/ACP integrations against real counterparties |

Known functional limits: the SPARQL timeout cannot kill a running worker thread; ambiguity detection is rule-based; the CNL template in the Studio cannot express "move some savings" transfers (use the CNL editor); `risk-review` clearing is a record only — the agent must resubmit.


See also: [security review](../security/security-review.md) (open items O-01 to O-21) and [risk register](../risk/risk-register.md) (strategic and adoption risks).
